Compounds: fn. 36, p. 126. Proclitics unstressed: p. 83.
catalog_quote: Observe in the data set below, for instance, that stress is always word-final in monomorphemic words and in prefixation. In cases involving prefixation, note that stress is preserved on the rightmost syllable, i.e. this word-formation process does not affect stress placement in the word. (39) Stress assignment in Picard: Word-final a. Monomorphemic words [os.ˈto] 'prison' [per.ˈtʃe] 'vegetable garden' [kra.vẽ.ˈʃõ] '(wild) plum' b. Prefixation [ˈprɔp] 'clean' [mal.ˈprɔp] 'dirty' ... In order to obey the restriction that Picard imposes on stress to be word-final, stress in monomorphemic words is shifted rightwards in derived forms, as illustrated below. (40) Stress assignment in suffixation: Word-final ... [ˈʒnu] 'knee' [ʒnu.ˈjer] 'patch (for knee area)' [me.ˈzõ] 'house' [me.zo.ˈnɛt] 'small, cute house' ... To capture the observation that word stress in Picard is consistently word-final, I adopt the alignment constraint AlignMWd/Ft, proposed by Bullock 1995 and adopted in her analysis of stress placement in French. ... To capture the fact that (1) stress is consistently assigned to the rightmost syllable of words, and that (2) words are maximally assigned one prominent syllable, I assume that the Foot in Picard is a non-iterative iamb (i.e. right-headed), and it is assigned to the rightmost edge of the word (by AlignMWd/Ft).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the final syllable of the (morphological) word; the foot is a single right-headed (iambic) foot aligned to the right edge, so each word has one prominent syllable. Suffixation shifts stress to the new final syllable (e.g. ['3nu] 'knee' vs [3nu.'jer]); prefixation leaves stress on the final syllable ([mal.'prop]); in compounds only the rightmost syllable keeps primary stress (fn. 36, p. 126). Examples from Vimeu Picard: [per.'tSe] 'vegetable garden', [me.'zo] 'house', [me.zo.'net] 'small house'. Author says stress assignment and foot form are 'similar to that of French' and notes a systematic study of the Picard foot system is outside the thesis's scope.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described; the foot is stated to be non-iterative (one foot per word), so no secondary stress is posited.
new_statements.exceptions: Proclitics (subject/object clitics, articles) are unstressed and unfooted in normal utterance; they can be stressed when uttered in isolation or focused (fn. 30-31, pp. 79-80). Compounds: only the rightmost member keeps primary stress (UNI-PEAK).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (Morphological Word = Prosodic Word), citation-type lexical items and derived words; Cardoso's analysis is prosodic-phonological (OT/Prosodic Phonology), based on Auger & Steele 1999, Auger p.c. and his own observations of Vimeu Picard speakers, not an instrumental study.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding source (Cardoso 2003) describes Vimeu Picard, the variety of the Vimeu region (Somme, France; villages Feuquières, Fressenneville, Bienfay, Bouillancourt, Nibas), which the author explicitly calls 'Picard' for expository reasons; no separate Glottolog dialect code known to me for Vimeu, so it is filed under pica1241. Cardoso states the pattern is 'similar to that of French' and relies partly on Auger & Steele 1999 / Auger p.c. (same Vimeu variety). Other varieties examined (Boulonnais: Haigneré 1901; Laonnais/Soissonnais: Bonnotte 1896; Démuin: Hrkal 1910; Cachy: Logie 1892) gave no synchronic stress statement.

tone.quote: La comparaison avec la durée moyenne calculée montre qu'il y a dans les deux corpus des allongements en syllabe pénultième, accompagnés d'une chute mélodique : c'est un trait caractéristique du picard du Nord [Car79], identifié comme un « accent traînant » [...] la voyelle pénultième est longue .Dans ces exemples, l'accent lexical est final, marqué par une forte proéminence mélodique. [...] Nous avons délimité té groupes accentuels en nous fondant sur le fait que l'accent est final de groupe. L'analyse instrumentale montre que celui-ci est réalisé par une proéminence mélodique accompagnée, sauf exception signalée, d'une durée et d'une intensité accrue.
tone.translation: Comparison with the computed mean duration shows that in both corpora there are lengthenings in the penultimate syllable, accompanied by a melodic fall: this is a characteristic trait of northern Picard [Car79], identified as a 'drawling accent' [...] the penultimate vowel is long. In these examples the lexical accent is final, marked by a strong melodic prominence. [...] We delimited the accent groups on the basis that the accent is group-final. Instrumental analysis shows that it is realised by a melodic prominence accompanied, unless otherwise noted, by increased duration and intensity.
tone.n_tones: None: pitch described only as accentual/intonational prominence, no tone invent…

tone.quote: L'accent qui frappe le second élément peut se porter sur le premier élément. Le lexème est alors accentué sur la pénultième, en conformité avec les règles d'accentuation de mot en néerlandais et en Wvl, dont les diphtongues sont descendantes (Booij 1999, 2). Exemple: [po'teo>po'teo] «copain».
tone.translation: The accent that falls on the second element may move to the first element. The lexeme is then stressed on the penultimate, in conformity with the word-accentuation rules of Dutch and West Flemish, whose diphthongs are falling (Booij 1999, 2). Example: [po'teo > po'teo] 'copain'.
tone.n_tones: None: phoneme system without tonemes; no tone section

sources.note: Per Auger 2017's summary it derives phonetic correlates of prosodic boundaries (10,000+ vowel durations, c. 700 pauses) to motivate Nespor & Vogel prosodic levels in Picard and shows prothesis, epithesis, denasalisation of 'point' and the floating /t/ of 'toute' are conditioned by prosodic domain, with group-final positions bearing a prosodic-group accent; a tone analysis is not expected, but the thesis is the fullest instrumental account of Picard prosodic structure.
